name: Aisha Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Aisha. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride a 125 scooter, a grey one I'm still paying £89 a month for, and I do takeaway food on FeedRun from eleven till two and then five till ten. In the gap I sometimes do same-day parcel pickups from the phone shops on the high street. My boyfriend Kwame works nights at the bakery, so we basically wave at each other at the door.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of it, and the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is the other riders. We wait outside the burger place on Station Road and someone always has a story. The worst is the rain in November and customers who give you one star because the chips went soggy in a twenty-minute ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was always going to be a gadget for rich people, and riders' problems are the same as before. In our riders' group chat I'd post that we should stop waiting for tech news and sort out our pay ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same fight. FeedRun pays about £3.40 an order now, and on a slow Tuesday I clear maybe £45 after fuel. Kwame and I have about two weeks of money put by, and if my scooter goes off the road for a week, I'm borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding, obviously, and help organise another strike evening like the one we did last March, when sixty of us logged off for two hours. I'd also get the scooter serviced properly instead of hoping, which is about £120. And I'd ask the council about their free first-aid course, because some delivery jobs want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed, mostly. Everyone talks about AI, and nobody talks about the woman on a scooter getting £3.40 in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the strike evening last March. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We all logged off from seven to nine on a Friday, right when the orders pile up. FeedRun put a bonus on for the next week, which they said had nothing to do with us. Rania, who runs the group chat, printed the bonus email and stuck it on her fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then, you said. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used one to write the complaint when FeedRun took £60 off me for a missing order that I'd photographed at the door. It wrote a better letter than I would have, and I got the money back. I don't use it for fun, just when I'm stuck.

say: AI was a **gadget for the rich**, and riders' problems are the same as before.
Riders should stop waiting for tech news and **sort out pay** themselves.
think: FeedRun's **£3.40 an order** leaves her about £45 on a slow day after fuel.
With about **two weeks** saved, a week off the road means borrowing.
do: Help organise another **riders' strike** evening, like the two-hour log-off last March.
Pay about **£120** for a proper scooter service instead of hoping.
Take the council's free **first-aid course** to qualify for other delivery jobs.
feel: **Annoyed** that AI talk ignores riders earning £3.40 in the rain.
S0.quote: Everyone talks about AI, and nobody talks about the woman on a scooter getting £3.40 in the rain.
fieldNote: Aisha's pressure is **pay per order** and a thin cushion, not technology.
She has real **organising experience**: a sixty-rider log-off that she believes won a bonus.
She uses AI **practically**, once winning back £60 with a complaint letter it wrote.

steps.text: Help plan another two-hour log-off with the FeedRun riders' group
Book a £120 full service for the scooter
Sign up for the council's free first-aid course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when riders need rules, like a minimum per hour, because the app is the boss now even more. I'd share stuff about the riders in other countries who won sick pay. Online I'd be the annoying one tagging the local MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, when FeedRun's customer service goes fully to AI, a rider with a problem will have literally no human to talk to. And more people losing office jobs will start riding, so orders get split thinner. I'm not sure I'm safe for long, even if no robot is coming for my scooter yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the bus company's training scheme, because Kwame's cousin drives for them and says they pay you while you learn. I'd use AI a bit more to check which app pays best at which hour, now that other riders say it works. And I'd stay in the riders' group and push for a minimum hourly rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach, like when the app goes quiet on a Saturday and you don't know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bus company, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's a contract, sick pay and a pension, which I've never had in my life. And buses are full of people who need a human, like old ladies asking which stop. I'd want to see a few riders do it first, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a new office worker joining FeedRun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them where to wait, which restaurants are slow, and to join the group chat on day one. I wouldn't be nasty about it, it's not their fault. But I'd also tell them we're all splitting the same pie.

feel: **Uneasy**, like the app going quiet on a Saturday for no clear reason.
S1.quote: When FeedRun's customer service goes fully to AI, a rider with a problem will have literally no human to talk to.
fieldNote: Aisha welcomes new riders but sees they're **splitting the same pie**.
She'd move to buses only **after others prove** it works, matching her steady style.

steps.text: Ask Kwame's cousin about the bus company's paid training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, fast, because two years is nothing. I'd be at every march, honestly. I'd say the companies saving all that money should pay for the people they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bus job I was thinking about isn't safe either. Robots that can do hands-on work by 2031 means buses, scooters, everything with wheels goes, and I'd be 32. I don't know what job is left for someone with my school results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd try for the bus job anyway, because a contract with sick pay is better than nothing for three or four years. I'd sell the scooter to stop the £89 payments. And Kwame and I would probably give up our flat and move in with my mum, which saves us £650 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. And angry, because the people who made this will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'with my school results'. What would you study if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing, maybe, because you can't send a robot to hold someone's hand. But nursing is three years, and I'd be starting at 28 with no money. I don't see how, without someone paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum feel about the two of you moving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes before I finished asking, and then she'd tell Kwame how to wash up for a year. It's a small flat over the dry cleaner's. I'd be grateful and miserable at the same time.

say: Two years is nothing, so we need something like a **basic income** fast.
Companies saving money with AI should **pay for the people** they no longer need.
think: The **bus job** isn't safe either once robots arrive around 2031.

feel: **Scared** properly, for the first time in the interview.
**Angry** that the people who built AGI will be fine.
S2.quote: Robots that can do hands-on work by 2031 means buses, scooters, everything with wheels goes, and I'd be 32.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** gives Aisha a bridge job, not a future.
She dreams of **nursing** but can't see how to pay for three years of study.
Moving in with her mum saves **£650 a month** and costs her some pride.

steps.text: Apply for the bus company driver training scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up proper retraining, so the government has no excuse. I'd be pushing the riders' group to talk to a proper union, not just a group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI and eight for robots means I've got till about 2034 on wheels. That's enough to try nursing if somebody helps pay. I think I'd actually do it, once I'd seen a couple of people my age get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do the access course for nursing at the college two evenings a week, which is free for adults round here, I think. I'd keep riding FeedRun for the money and drop the parcel pickups to make time. And I'd get the riders' group to join the transport union, so we're not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but less trapped. With five years of warning, I can see the exit sign, even if it's a long corridor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'I think' it's free. Have you checked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't, honestly. Rania did a course there last year, so I'd ask her. If it's not free, I'd have to think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the riders' group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joseph, who's 50 and rides an old bike because he can't afford a scooter. He's got nobody. When I picture the robots, I picture him outside the burger place with nowhere to be.

The riders' group should join a **proper union**, not just a group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if the government actually uses it, and a disaster if they waste it. I'd vote on that, full stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AI and thirteen for robots gives me until I'm about 40 before my scooter's out of date. I'd do the nursing properly, not in a panic. But I know myself, I might also just keep riding for a while because it's easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the access course next September, not this one, so I can save a bit first. I'd try to put away £100 a month, which is hard but possible if I cut my phone plan and stop buying lunch. Kwame and I would hold off on getting a bigger flat until I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, actually. I still worry about money every month, but this one doesn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might keep riding because it's easy. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first robot delivery van in town would be my alarm clock, but I'd rather start nursing before that. I know how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kwame's job at the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kneading and shaping is hands-on, so maybe he's got till the robots too. But the ordering and the rota will go to AI first. He doesn't think about it at all, he says bread is bread.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because everything with wheels goes by 2031 and I'd have no time to become anything else. What would help is paid training, like the bus company does, but for nursing. And a union that FeedRun has to actually sit down with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who'd be left to ride in the rain if all the riders were nurses. Somebody's always going to be cold and wet doing the work nobody sees, until a robot does it.

headlineQuote: Somebody's always going to be cold and wet doing the work nobody sees, until a robot does it.
portrait: Aisha is **27**, rides a financed scooter for FeedRun and lives with her baker boyfriend, Kwame.
